source.title: Beyond Sharpness: A Flatness Decomposition Framework for Efficient Continual Learning
source.authors: Yanan Chen; Tie-Liang Gong; Yunjiao Zhang; Wen Wen

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and supplementary material; no relevant section appears cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It studies sharpness-aware optimization and generalization in continual-learning settings, extending the topic to a new training setting. It does not test the listed versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports continual-learning accuracies and flatness measurements for its own method and related optimizer variants. Those findings do not measure the train-test gap, magnitude-aware sharpness, or the specific interventions named in V1–V8. Cited findings from earlier work are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.3 reports an original batch-size sweep with GAM: smaller batches consistently improve average accuracy. This bears on V5 in a continual-learning setting. The general implementation specifies 170 epochs for sharpness-aware optimizers, although A.3 does not explicitly confirm the sweep's epoch budget. The curvature diagnostics and FLAD performance comparisons do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that isolating stochastic-noise components promotes flatter solutions and improves continual-learning performance, and that partial application preserves gains while reducing overhead.
record.recipe_differences: Uses decomposed sharpness-aware perturbations in continual class-incremental learning, compares against SGD and continual-learning optimizers, and reports accuracy, flatness, and computational results rather than train-test generalization gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes GAM accuracy: the text says smaller batches consistently improve generalization, while excessively small batches use hardware inefficiently; batch size 128 is described as a favorable trade-off. FLAD perturbation direction affects accuracy, and its Tr(HΣ) trend differs between early and later training.

fits_no_version.finding: Noise-directed perturbations outperform the other tested directions, while the full-gradient variant degrades performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Isolating stochastic-noise perturbations can improve accuracy in the tested continual-learning settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Noise variants alter curvature–noise alignment during training and produce flatter final landscapes; FLAD also reduces Hessian eigenvalues and trace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FLAD's noise decomposition changes curvature diagnostics and promotes flatter solutions in these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports positive aggregate returns for FLAD over C-Flat across six continual-learning methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FLAD improves aggregate continual-learning accuracy over C-Flat across the reported methods.

record.problems: The reported outcomes concern continual-learning accuracy rather than an explicit training-versus-test error gap. Several diagnostic comparisons are described only through figures without numeric values. The batch-size sweep does not state the dataset in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 contains separate Acc and AAA values for each dataset and task setting across six CL methods; those per-setting entries were not extracted because the table's aggregate Average Return values provide the reported cross-setting comparison within the 60-row limit. Figures 3–5 report ablations and efficiency results not mapped to a listed version and were left out.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Workload-dependent thresholds, language models, and remedies involving longer training, scaling, warmup, normalization or regularization. The sweep does not explicitly document its epoch budget, dataset or architecture.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence and removal alongside weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, similarly low training loss, measured train–test gaps and ranking against norm- or margin-based measures.
Memorization-based example removal versus equally sized random removal.

missing.what: Add a sweep-level result recording the explicitly stated improvement with smaller batches. The existing per-batch rows contain no readable outcome values, although their notes mention the trend.
missing.locator: Appendix A.3, Effect of batchsize; Figure A1

record.verdict_notes: An explicit train–test gap is required for V7, but V5 concerns held-out performance and can be informed by the reported average-accuracy sweep. The record therefore incorrectly excludes the batch-size results from every version. All judgments use only the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected network comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Large-batch versus small-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

relationships.condition: GAM batch-size sweep from 8 to 256 in Appendix A.3.
relationships.reason: The text accompanying R17–R21 explicitly reports better generalization with smaller batches. This verdict rests on that textual trend, not readable individual accuracies; fixed epochs are suggested by the general 170-epoch recipe but are not confirmed for this sweep.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports better generalization with smaller batches, but the comparison remains unverified and equal epoch budgets were unconfirmed.
